answers.question: Process vs Thread — memory space, stack, overhead
answers.shortTitle: Process vs Thread — memory space, stack, overhead

s1_definition.profdef: A **process** is an independent running program with its own ISOLATED memory space (heap, code segment, data segment). Each process gets its own address space from the OS. If one process crashes, others continue running. Communication between processes requires IPC (Inter-Process Communication) — sockets, pipes, shared memory — which is relatively expensive. A **thread** is a lightweight unit of execution WITHIN a process. All threads in a process SHARE the same heap memory, but each thread has its OWN stack (local variables, method calls). Threads are cheaper to create (~1MB stack, ~1ms) vs processes (~100ms). The trade-off: shared memory enables fast communication but requires SYNCHRONIZATION to prevent data corruption.
s1_definition.analogy: A **process** is a separate bank BRANCH — own building, own vault, own staff. If one branch burns down, other branches continue operating. Communication between branches: slow mail/courier (IPC). A **thread** is an employee WITHIN one branch. All employees share the same vault (heap memory) and can access any drawer. But if two employees try to update the SAME account register simultaneously without coordinating (synchronization), the register gets corrupted. Each employee has their own desk with personal notes (own stack).
s1_definition.oneliner: Process = own memory, isolated, heavy, crash-safe. Thread = shared heap, own stack, lightweight, needs synchronization. Threads share data fast but must coordinate access.

A **thread** is a lightweight unit of execution WITHIN a process. All threads in a process SHARE the same heap memory, but each thread has its OWN stack (local variables, method calls). Threads are cheaper to create (~1MB stack, ~1ms) vs processes (~100ms). The trade-off: shared memory enables fast communication but requires SYNCHRONIZATION to prevent data corruption.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A **process** is a separate bank BRANCH — own building, own vault, own staff. If one branch burns down, other branches continue operating. **One line to remember:** Process = own memory, isolated, heavy, crash-safe. Thread = shared heap, own stack, lightweight, needs synchronization. Threads share data fast but must coordinate access.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's trading platform needs to handle 10,000 concurrent trade orders per second.** Using separate processes for each order: 10,000 processes × 100MB = 1TB RAM — impossible. Fix: ONE process (JVM) with 200 threads. Each thread handles one trade order. All threads share the order book (heap memory). Thread creation: ~1ms each. Communication: direct shared memory access (nanoseconds). But: shared order book needs synchronization — two threads can't modify the same order simultaneously.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
mvn clean test
# ProcessVsThreadTest: 4 tests — all pass!
```
sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** JVM process starts — OS allocates memory (heap + metaspace). One main thread created.

**Step 2.** Main thread creates 10 worker threads. Each thread gets its own stack (~1MB). All share the same heap.

**Step 3.** All 10 threads increment a shared AtomicInteger. Each thread reads the counter, atomically increments, writes back. No race condition because AtomicInteger uses CAS (Compare-And-Swap).

**Step 4.** Without AtomicInteger: two threads read balance=100000 simultaneously, both compute 99000, both write 99000. One decrement LOST. With AtomicInteger: CAS ensures only one thread's write succeeds; the other retries.

```
  Fix: AtomicInteger.addAndGet(-50000) → CAS → only one succeeds, other retries.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A process is an independent program with its own memory space — heap, code, data segment — fully isolated from other processes. If one process crashes, others survive. Communication between processes requires IPC (sockets, pipes, Kafka) which is relatively slow. A thread is a lightweight execution unit within a process — all threads share the same heap but each has its own stack. Thread creation is fast (~1ms, ~1MB stack) vs process creation (~100ms, ~100MB).

The trade-off: threads share memory so they can communicate instantly (nanoseconds) by reading/writing shared objects, but this requires synchronization (synchronized, Lock, Atomic classes) to prevent race conditions. Without synchronization, two threads reading and modifying the same balance simultaneously can lose updates — debiting Rs.50,000 twice but the balance only reflects one debit. In banking: one JVM process with 200 threads handles 10K trade orders/sec. Threads share the order book (ConcurrentHashMap), balance cache (AtomicInteger), and trade queue (LinkedBlockingQueue). Separate processes (via Kafka) for settlement and notification — isolated, crash-safe.

answers.question: Ways to create a thread — Thread, Runnable, Callable/ExecutorService — which is preferred
answers.shortTitle: Ways to create a thread — Thread, Runnable, Callable/ExecutorService — which is preferred

s1_definition.profdef: Java offers three ways to create threads: (1) **Extend Thread class** — override `run()`, call `start()`. Simple but bad: your class can't extend anything else (Java has single inheritance). (2) **Implement Runnable** — implement `run()`, pass to `new Thread(runnable).start()`. Preferred: separates the TASK (what to do) from the THREAD (how to run it). Can also submit to ExecutorService (thread pool). (3) **Implement Callable<V> + ExecutorService** — like Runnable but returns a result (`V call()`) and can throw checked exceptions. Submit to ExecutorService, get a `Future<V>` to retrieve the result. **Preferred approach**: Runnable/Callable + ExecutorService (thread pool). NEVER create raw threads in production — thread pools manage lifecycle, limit concurrency, and reuse threads.
s1_definition.analogy: (1) **Extend Thread** = each bank teller IS a person AND a task — they can only do one type of job (single inheritance limitation). (2) **Implement Runnable** = a TASK FORM (Runnable) given to any available teller (Thread). The form describes WHAT to do. Any teller can execute it. Better: separate the task from the person. (3) **Callable + ExecutorService** = a task form that RETURNS A RECEIPT (Future). You submit the form to the BANK COUNTER (thread pool), get a receipt number, and come back later to collect the result. Best: managed, efficient, returns results.
s1_definition.oneliner: Extend Thread = bad (single inheritance). Implement Runnable = good (task separated from thread). Callable + ExecutorService = best (returns result, managed pool, production-ready).

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The trade settlement service needed to process 5,000 trades per second.** A junior developer used `new Thread(() -> settle(trade)).start()` for each trade. Within 30 seconds: 150,000 threads created → `OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread`. Fix: `ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(100)` — 100 threads process trades from a queue. Trades submitted via `pool.submit(new TradeSettler(trade))`. Returns `Future<SettlementResult>` — the API can check status or block for result. Thread reuse: 100 threads handle 5,000 trades/sec. No OOM.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
mvn clean test
# ThreadCreationTest: 5 tests — all pass!
```
sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Application creates an ExecutorService with 4 threads: `newFixedThreadPool(4)`. Four worker threads are created and IDLE, waiting for tasks.

**Step 2.** 10 Callable tasks submitted via `pool.submit()`. Each returns a `Future<String>`. Tasks are queued in the pool's internal LinkedBlockingQueue.

**Step 3.** The 4 threads pick up tasks from the queue. Thread-1 takes TRD-001, Thread-2 takes TRD-002, Thread-3 takes TRD-003, Thread-4 takes TRD-004. When Thread-1 finishes TRD-001, it picks up TRD-005 (reuse!).

**Step 4.** Each `future.get()` blocks until the corresponding task completes. The result ("SETTLED:TRD-001") is stored in the Future object by the worker thread.

**Step 5.** All 10 results collected. `pool.shutdown()` stops accepting new tasks and waits for running tasks to finish.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ THREAD CREATION: 3 WAYS ═══

  WAY 1: Extend Thread (BAD)
  class MyThread extends Thread { void run() {...} }
  new MyThread().start();
  Problem: single inheritance, task coupled to thread.

  WAY 2: Implement Runnable (GOOD)
  Runnable task = () -> settle(trade);
  new Thread(task).start();   OR   pool.submit(task);
  Better: task separated from thread. No return value.

  WAY 3: Callable + ExecutorService (BEST)
  Callable<String> task = () -> { return settle(trade); };
  Future<String> f = pool.submit(task);
  String result = f.get();
  Best: returns result, throws exceptions, managed pool.

  ═══ THREAD POOL FLOW ═══
  submit(task1) → Queue: [task1, task2, task3, ...]
                    ↓
  Pool: [Thread-1] [Thread-2] [Thread-3] [Thread-4]
         picks       picks      picks      picks
         task1       task2      task3      task4
         done→picks  done→picks
         task5       task6     ...
  4 threads process 10 tasks via REUSE!
```

```
  └──────────┘         │  ExecutorService (100 threads)   │
                       │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐│
                       │  │ BlockingQueue (task queue)   ││
                       │  │ [Callable1][Callable2][...]  ││
                       │  └──────────┬──────────────────┘│
                       │   Thread-1 ↓  Thread-2 ↓  ...  │
                       │   settle()    settle()          │
                       │   Future<Result>                │
                       └──────────┬──────────────────────┘
                                  │ JDBC
                       ┌──────────▼──────────────────────┐
                       │  PostgreSQL (trades, accounts)   │
                       └──────────────────────────────────┘
  5000 trades/sec → queued → 100 threads process → reuse → no OOM
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Thread Creation Approaches ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │      <<interface>>             │
  │      Runnable                  │
  │  ──────────────────────────── │
  │  + run(): void                │  no return, no checked exception
  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                  │ implements
  ┌───────────────▼───────────────┐
  │      TradeTask                 │
  │  - tradeId: String            │
  │  + run(): void                │
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │      <<interface>>             │
  │      Callable<V>               │
  │  ──────────────────────────── │
  │  + call(): V throws Exception │  returns result + throws!
  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                  │ implements
  ┌───────────────▼───────────────┐
  │      TradeSettler              │
  │  - tradeId: String            │
  │  + call(): String             │  returns "SETTLED:TRD-001"
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │      ExecutorService           │  ← Thread pool manager
  │  ──────────────────────────── │
  │  + submit(Callable): Future   │
  │  + submit(Runnable): Future   │
  │  + shutdown(): void           │
  │  Internal: BlockingQueue      │  tasks wait here
  │  Internal: Thread[poolSize]   │  worker threads
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. pool.submit(new TradeSettler("TRD-001"))
  2. → task queued in BlockingQueue
  3. → idle Thread picks task → calls settler.call()
  4. → result stored in Future
  5. → caller: future.get() → "SETTLED:TRD-001"
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Three ways to create threads: extending Thread (bad — single inheritance, task coupled to thread), implementing Runnable (good — task separated, but no return value or checked exceptions), and Callable with ExecutorService (best — returns Future with result, throws checked exceptions, managed thread pool). In production, NEVER create raw threads with `new Thread().start()` — use ExecutorService. Raw threads have no limit (OOM with thousands of threads), no reuse (creation cost per request), and no monitoring.

ExecutorService provides: fixed thread pool size (limits concurrency), task queue (back-pressure when threads are busy), thread reuse (one thread handles thousands of tasks), and Future for asynchronous result retrieval. `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(100)` creates 100 reusable threads. `pool.submit(callable)` returns `Future<V>` — call `future.get()` to block for the result. In banking: trade settlement — 5,000 trades/sec → 100-thread pool → each thread processes ~50 trades/sec → thread reuse → no OOM, predictable resource usage.

answers.question: Thread lifecycle / states — New, Runnable, Blocked, Waiting, Timed Waiting, Terminated
answers.shortTitle: Thread lifecycle / states — New, Runnable, Blocked, Waiting, Timed Waiting, Terminated

s1_definition.profdef: A Java thread goes through 6 states defined in `Thread.State` enum: (1) **NEW** — created but `start()` not yet called. (2) **RUNNABLE** — eligible to run; may be executing on CPU or waiting for CPU time from the OS scheduler. (3) **BLOCKED** — waiting to acquire a monitor lock (trying to enter a `synchronized` block held by another thread). (4) **WAITING** — voluntarily waiting indefinitely until another thread signals: `wait()`, `join()`, `LockSupport.park()`. (5) **TIMED_WAITING** — waiting with a timeout: `sleep(millis)`, `wait(millis)`, `join(millis)`. (6) **TERMINATED** — `run()` has completed (normally or via exception). A terminated thread CANNOT be restarted — calling `start()` again throws `IllegalThreadStateException`. You must create a NEW Thread object.
s1_definition.analogy: A bank teller's workday: **NEW** = hired but hasn't shown up for first day yet. **RUNNABLE** = at the counter, ready to serve (or waiting in line for a free counter/CPU). **BLOCKED** = standing at the vault door waiting for another teller to leave (synchronized lock). **WAITING** = sitting in the break room waiting for the manager to call them back (wait/notify). **TIMED_WAITING** = on a 30-minute lunch break — comes back after the timer (sleep/wait with timeout). **TERMINATED** = retired. Cannot un-retire! Must hire a new teller (new Thread).
s1_definition.oneliner: NEW → start() → RUNNABLE ↔ BLOCKED/WAITING/TIMED_WAITING → run() ends → TERMINATED. Terminated = permanent. Cannot restart. Create new Thread.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Java thread goes through 6 states defined in `Thread.State` enum: (1) **NEW** — created but `start()` not yet called. (2) **RUNNABLE** — eligible to run; may be executing on CPU or waiting for CPU time from the OS scheduler. (3) **BLOCKED** — waiting to acquire a monitor lock (trying to enter a `synchronized` block held by another thread). (4) **WAITING** — voluntarily waiting indefinitely until another thread signals: `wait()`, `join()`, `LockSupport.park()`. (5) **TIMED_WAITING** — waiting with a timeout: `sleep(millis)`, `wait(millis)`, `join(millis)`. (6) **TERMINATED** — `run()` has completed (normally or via exception). A terminated thread CANNOT be restarted — calling `start()` again throws `IllegalThreadStateException`. You must create a NEW Thread object.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A bank teller's workday: **NEW** = hired but hasn't shown up for first day yet. **RUNNABLE** = at the counter, ready to serve (or waiting in line for a free counter/CPU). **BLOCKED** = standing at the vault door waiting for another teller to leave (synchronized lock). **WAITING** = sitting in the break room waiting for the manager to call them back (wait/notify). **TIMED_WAITING** = on a 30-minute lunch break — comes back after the timer (sleep/wait with timeout). **TERMINATED** = retired. Cannot un-retire! Must hire a new teller (new Thread).

**One line to remember:** NEW → start() → RUNNABLE ↔ BLOCKED/WAITING/TIMED_WAITING → run() ends → TERMINATED. Terminated = permanent. Cannot restart. Create new Thread.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The operations team wanted a dashboard showing thread states for the trade processing pool.** They needed to know: how many threads are RUNNABLE (actively processing trades), how many are BLOCKED (waiting for database locks), how many are WAITING (idle in pool waiting for tasks), and how many are TERMINATED (crashed). This data helps diagnose performance bottlenecks: many BLOCKED threads = database contention. Many WAITING threads = not enough work or slow upstream.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
mvn clean test
# ThreadLifecycleTest: 6 tests — all pass!
```
sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** `new Thread(task)` → state = NEW. Thread object created in heap, but no OS thread exists yet.

**Step 2.** `t.start()` → state = RUNNABLE. JVM creates an OS thread. Thread is eligible for CPU time. The OS scheduler decides when it actually runs.

**Step 3.** Thread tries to enter `synchronized(lock)` but lock is held → state = BLOCKED. Thread waits in the lock's entry set until the lock is released.

**Step 4.** Thread calls `lock.wait()` → state = WAITING. Thread releases the lock and enters the lock's wait set. Another thread must call `lock.notify()` to wake it.

**Step 5.** Thread calls `Thread.sleep(5000)` → state = TIMED_WAITING. Thread pauses for 5 seconds, then automatically returns to RUNNABLE.

**Step 6.** `run()` completes → state = TERMINATED. Thread is dead. Calling `start()` again throws IllegalThreadStateException. Must create a new Thread object.

```
  ═══ THREAD LIFECYCLE STATE DIAGRAM ═══

        NEW ───────────────────→ RUNNABLE ──── run() ends ──→ TERMINATED
                                   ↑  │  ↑                    (PERMANENT)
                          lock     │  │  │ lock                Cannot restart!
                        acquired   │  │  │ contention
                                   │  │  │
                              ┌────┘  │  └────┐
                              │       │       │
                          RUNNABLE  ←─┘   BLOCKED
                              ↑               (waiting for
                    notify/   │               monitor lock)
                    unpark    │
                              │  wait()/join()/park()
                          WAITING
                      (indefinite wait)

                    timeout   ↑
                    expires   │  sleep(ms)/wait(ms)/join(ms)
                              │
                       TIMED_WAITING
                       (wait with timeout)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Thread.State Enum + Transitions ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │       Thread                  │
  │  ──────────────────────────  │
  │  - target: Runnable          │
  │  - state: Thread.State       │
  │  - name: String              │
  │  - daemon: boolean           │
  │  ──────────────────────────  │
  │  + start(): void             │  NEW → RUNNABLE (creates OS thread)
  │  + run(): void               │  executes target.run()
  │  + join(): void              │  caller enters WAITING until this terminates
  │  + sleep(ms): static void    │  current thread → TIMED_WAITING
  │  + getState(): Thread.State  │  returns current state
  │  + interrupt(): void         │  sets interrupt flag
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │   <<enum>> Thread.State      │
  │  ──────────────────────────  │
  │  NEW                         │  created, not started
  │  RUNNABLE                    │  running or ready to run
  │  BLOCKED                     │  waiting for monitor lock
  │  WAITING                     │  wait()/join()/park()
  │  TIMED_WAITING               │  sleep(ms)/wait(ms)/join(ms)
  │  TERMINATED                  │  run() completed, cannot restart
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  Transition triggers:
  NEW → RUNNABLE:        start()
  RUNNABLE → BLOCKED:    entering synchronized (lock held)
  BLOCKED → RUNNABLE:    lock acquired
  RUNNABLE → WAITING:    wait()/join()/park()
  WAITING → RUNNABLE:    notify()/notifyAll()/unpark()
  RUNNABLE → TIMED_WAIT: sleep(ms)/wait(ms)/join(ms)
  TIMED_WAIT → RUNNABLE: timeout expires / notify()
  RUNNABLE → TERMINATED: run() completes
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Java thread has 6 states in the `Thread.State` enum. NEW: created but start() not called. RUNNABLE: running or ready for CPU time (Java doesn't distinguish "running" vs "ready" — both are RUNNABLE). BLOCKED: involuntary wait for a monitor lock (another thread holds the synchronized lock). WAITING: voluntary indefinite wait — thread called wait(), join(), or park() and waits for explicit signal (notify, unpark, or joined thread termination). TIMED_WAITING: voluntary wait with timeout — sleep(ms), wait(ms), join(ms) — automatically returns to RUNNABLE when timeout expires.

TERMINATED: run() completed (normally or via uncaught exception). A terminated thread CANNOT be restarted — calling start() throws IllegalThreadStateException. You must create a new Thread object with the same Runnable. In banking: monitoring thread pool states reveals performance issues — many BLOCKED threads indicate database lock contention (fix: optimize queries, reduce transaction scope). Many TIMED_WAITING threads indicate idle pool (normal during low traffic). Zero RUNNABLE threads with a full task queue indicates a deadlock (emergency: thread dump analysis).

answers.question: BLOCKED vs WAITING thread states — involuntary lock wait vs voluntary signal wait
answers.shortTitle: BLOCKED vs WAITING thread states — involuntary lock wait vs voluntary signal wait

s1_definition.profdef: **BLOCKED** = involuntary — a thread is trying to enter a `synchronized` block or method, but ANOTHER thread already holds that monitor lock. The blocked thread has NO CHOICE but to wait until the lock is released. It didn't ASK to wait — it was FORCED by lock contention. **WAITING** = voluntary — a thread CHOSE to wait by calling `wait()`, `join()`, or `LockSupport.park()`. It gave up the CPU deliberately and will only resume when another thread explicitly signals it (`notify()`, `notifyAll()`, `unpark()`, or the joined thread terminates). Key difference: BLOCKED threads compete for a lock (involuntary). WAITING threads cooperate through signaling (voluntary). A BLOCKED thread automatically resumes when the lock is free. A WAITING thread requires an explicit wake-up signal.
s1_definition.analogy: **BLOCKED** = you arrive at the vault door but it's LOCKED by another teller inside. You MUST stand outside and wait — no choice. The moment the other teller exits (releases lock), you enter automatically. **WAITING** = you VOLUNTARILY sit in the break room and tell the manager "call me when the VIP client arrives" (wait/notify). You chose to wait. You won't get up until the manager explicitly calls you (notify). Nobody forced you to sit — you decided to wait for a specific event.
s1_definition.oneliner: BLOCKED = forced wait for lock (involuntary, auto-resumes when lock free). WAITING = chosen wait for signal (voluntary, needs explicit notify/unpark to resume).

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The trade settlement service had 50 threads processing trades.** Thread dump showed: 30 threads in BLOCKED state (all waiting for `synchronized(accountLock)` — one slow database query held the lock for 500ms). 15 threads in WAITING state (idle in the thread pool waiting for tasks — `queue.take()` → WAITING). Only 5 threads RUNNABLE. Diagnosis: BLOCKED threads indicate lock contention (fix: reduce synchronized scope, use ReadWriteLock). WAITING threads are normal for idle pool workers.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
mvn clean test
# BlockedVsWaitingTest: 4 tests — all pass!
```
sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Thread-1 enters `synchronized(lock)` and holds the lock. It then calls `Thread.sleep(5000)` — state = TIMED_WAITING but lock is NOT released.

**Step 2.** Thread-2 tries to enter `synchronized(lock)` — state = BLOCKED. It cannot acquire the lock because Thread-1 holds it. Thread-2 is placed in the lock's entry set.

**Step 3.** Thread-3 enters `synchronized(lock)` and calls `lock.wait()` — state = WAITING. The lock IS released. Thread-3 is placed in the lock's wait set.

**Step 4.** Thread-1 finishes sleep, exits synchronized → lock released. Thread-2 (BLOCKED) automatically acquires lock → RUNNABLE. Thread-3 (WAITING) still waits — needs explicit notify().

**Step 5.** Thread-2 calls `lock.notify()` → Thread-3 moves from wait set to entry set. When Thread-2 exits synchronized → Thread-3 acquires lock → RUNNABLE.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ BLOCKED vs WAITING ═══

  BLOCKED (involuntary):
  Thread-2 → synchronized(lock) → lock held by Thread-1 → BLOCKED!
  Thread-1 exits → lock free → Thread-2 auto-acquires → RUNNABLE
  Thread-2 did NOT choose to wait. It was FORCED by lock contention.

  WAITING (voluntary):
  Thread-3 → synchronized(lock) → lock.wait() → RELEASES lock → WAITING
  Another thread: lock.notify() → Thread-3 moves to entry set → acquires lock → RUNNABLE
  Thread-3 CHOSE to wait. It needs explicit notify() to resume.

  ═══ wait() vs sleep() — CRITICAL DIFFERENCE ═══

  synchronized (lock) {
      lock.wait();         // RELEASES lock! Others CAN enter.
      Thread.sleep(5000);  // does NOT release lock! Others BLOCKED!
  }

  ═══ LOCK SETS ═══
  Entry Set: threads waiting to ACQUIRE lock  → BLOCKED state
  Wait Set:  threads that called wait()       → WAITING state
  notify() moves ONE thread: wait set → entry set
  notifyAll() moves ALL threads: wait set → entry set
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Monitor Lock: Entry Set vs Wait Set ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           Object Monitor (lock)            │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  Owner: Thread-1 (holds lock)             │
  │                                            │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐                  │
  │  │ Entry Set (BLOCKED) │                  │
  │  │ Thread-2, Thread-4  │ → waiting to     │
  │  │                     │   ACQUIRE lock   │
  │  └─────────────────────┘                  │
  │                                            │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐                  │
  │  │ Wait Set (WAITING)  │                  │
  │  │ Thread-3, Thread-5  │ → called wait(), │
  │  │                     │   RELEASED lock  │
  │  └─────────────────────┘                  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘

  notify():     moves ONE from Wait Set → Entry Set
  notifyAll():  moves ALL from Wait Set → Entry Set
  Lock release: ONE from Entry Set acquires lock → RUNNABLE

  Transition: WAITING →notify→ Entry Set →lock free→ RUNNABLE
              BLOCKED →lock released→ RUNNABLE (auto)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
BLOCKED and WAITING are both "not running" states, but they differ fundamentally. BLOCKED is involuntary — the thread tried to enter a synchronized block but another thread holds the lock. It automatically resumes when the lock is released. WAITING is voluntary — the thread explicitly called wait(), join(), or park(), releasing the lock (in the case of wait), and waits for an explicit signal (notify, notifyAll, unpark, or joined thread completion).

The critical detail: `wait()` RELEASES the monitor lock, allowing other threads to enter the synchronized block. `Thread.sleep()` does NOT release the lock — other threads remain BLOCKED while the sleeping thread holds the lock. Every Java object has a monitor with two sets: the entry set (BLOCKED threads waiting to acquire) and the wait set (WAITING threads that called wait()). `notify()` moves one thread from wait set to entry set. `notifyAll()` moves all. In banking: a thread dump showing 30 BLOCKED threads on the same lock = lock contention bottleneck. Fix: reduce synchronized scope, use ReadWriteLock (multiple readers concurrently), or use lock-free structures (ConcurrentHashMap, AtomicInteger).

answers.question: start() vs run() — calling run() directly does NOT create a new thread
answers.shortTitle: start() vs run() — calling run() directly does NOT create a new thread

s1_definition.profdef: `start()` creates a NEW OS thread, then the JVM calls `run()` on that new thread. The caller continues in parallel — true multithreading. `run()` called directly is just a NORMAL METHOD CALL on the CURRENT thread — no new thread is created, no parallelism, no concurrency. It executes sequentially like any other method. This is one of the most common beginner mistakes: calling `thread.run()` instead of `thread.start()` and wondering why code isn't running in parallel. `start()` can only be called ONCE — calling it twice throws `IllegalThreadStateException`.
s1_definition.analogy: `start()` = hiring a NEW teller and telling them "go serve customers at your counter" — the new teller works IN PARALLEL with you. Both of you serve customers simultaneously. `run()` = you YOURSELF do the teller's job at THEIR counter — you leave YOUR counter, go to their counter, do the work, come back. No new teller hired. No parallelism. You just did extra work sequentially.
s1_definition.oneliner: start() = new OS thread + calls run() on it (parallel). run() directly = no new thread, just a method call on current thread (sequential). ALWAYS use start(), NEVER call run() directly.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — A developer wrote a batch trade processor that called `tradeThread.run()` instead of `tradeThread.start()`.** Expected: 10 trade batches processed in PARALLEL (~100ms total). Actual: 10 batches processed SEQUENTIALLY (~1000ms total). The batch ran on the main thread — no parallelism. Thread dump showed only ONE thread doing all the work. Fix: changed `run()` to `start()`. 10x faster.

```bash
mvn clean test
# StartVsRunTest: 5 tests — all pass!
```
sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** `new Thread(task)` creates a Thread object in the heap. State = NEW. No OS thread exists yet.

**Step 2a (start).** `t.start()` → JVM calls native `start0()` → OS creates a new thread → new thread calls `t.run()` → task executes on the NEW thread. Main thread continues immediately — PARALLEL.

**Step 2b (run).** `t.run()` → Java calls the `run()` method directly on the CURRENT thread → task executes on the MAIN thread. Main thread is BLOCKED until run() finishes — SEQUENTIAL.

**Step 3.** With start(): 3 threads sleeping 100ms each → all sleep in PARALLEL → total ~100ms. With run(): 3 sequential sleeps → total ~300ms.

```
  ═══ start() — NEW THREAD (parallel) ═══

  Main thread: ──start()──→ continues immediately ──→ ...
                    │
                    └──→ NEW Thread-0: ──run()──→ task executes ──→ terminates
  Both run simultaneously!

  ═══ run() — SAME THREAD (sequential) ═══

  Main thread: ──run()──→ task executes ──→ returns ──→ continues
  NO new thread! Main thread does ALL the work!

  ═══ TIMING PROOF ═══
  3 × start() + sleep(100ms each): ~100ms total (parallel!)
  3 × run()   + sleep(100ms each): ~300ms total (sequential!)
```

```
                         │  │Batch-A │ │Batch-B │ │Bat-C ││
                         │  └────────┘ └────────┘ └──────┘│
                         │  All 3 batches: ~100ms total     │
                         │                                  │
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Thread.start() vs Thread.run() ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
  │           Thread                   │
  │  ──────────────────────────────── │
  │  - target: Runnable               │
  │  - threadStatus: int (state)      │
  │  - name: String                   │
  │  ──────────────────────────────── │
  │  + start(): void                  │
  │    1. if state != NEW → throw ISE │
  │    2. group.add(this)             │
  │    3. start0() (native)           │  ← OS creates thread
  │       → OS thread calls run()    │
  │    4. caller returns immediately  │  ← parallel!
  │                                    │
  │  + run(): void                    │
  │    if (target != null)            │
  │      target.run();                │  ← just a method call
  │    // runs on CALLER's thread     │  ← sequential!
  └───────────────────────────────────┘

  start() call chain:
  1. Java: thread.start()
  2. JVM:  start0() (native method)
  3. OS:   pthread_create() / CreateThread()
  4. New OS thread → calls Thread.run()
  5. run() calls target.run() (the Runnable)
  6. target.run() completes → thread state = TERMINATED
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
`start()` creates a new OS thread and calls `run()` on that new thread — the caller continues immediately, enabling true parallel execution. `run()` called directly is just a regular method call on the current thread — no new thread, no parallelism, no concurrency. This is one of the most common multithreading bugs: calling `run()` instead of `start()` and getting sequential execution instead of parallel.

Internally, `start()` checks the thread state (must be NEW), then calls native `start0()` which creates a real OS thread (via `pthread_create` on Linux, `CreateThread` on Windows). The new OS thread then invokes `run()`. `start()` can only be called once — calling it on a RUNNABLE or TERMINATED thread throws `IllegalThreadStateException`. In banking: a batch processor calling `run()` instead of `start()` processed 10 trade batches sequentially in 1000ms instead of in parallel in 100ms — a 10x performance regression caused by a one-character bug (missing "start" → "run").

answers.question: Synchronized method vs synchronized block — scope, lock object, granularity
answers.shortTitle: Synchronized method vs synchronized block — scope, lock object, granularity

s1_definition.profdef: **Synchronized method**: `public synchronized void transfer()` — locks on `this` (the entire object instance) for the ENTIRE method duration. For static methods: locks on `Class` object (`ClassName.class`). Simple but COARSE — the entire method body is locked, even parts that don't need synchronization. **Synchronized block**: `synchronized(lockObject) { /* critical section */ }` — locks on ANY specified object for ONLY the critical section. FINER granularity — only the code that accesses shared state is locked. Non-critical code runs without holding the lock. Block is preferred: you control WHICH lock, HOW LONG it's held, and WHAT is protected.
s1_definition.analogy: **Synchronized method** = locking the ENTIRE bank branch (the whole object) every time ONE teller needs to access the vault. Nobody can do ANYTHING — not even use the photocopier — until the vault operation finishes. **Synchronized block** = locking ONLY the vault door (specific lock object) for ONLY the time you're inside the vault. Other tellers can use the photocopier, answer phones, serve customers at other counters — everything outside the vault continues.
s1_definition.oneliner: Synchronized method = locks `this` for entire method (coarse). Synchronized block = locks specific object for specific code (fine). Block preferred — shorter lock time, specific lock, better concurrency.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** **Synchronized method**: `public synchronized void transfer()` — locks on `this` (the entire object instance) for the ENTIRE method duration. For static methods: locks on `Class` object (`ClassName.class`). Simple but COARSE — the entire method body is locked, even parts that don't need synchronization. **Synchronized block**: `synchronized(lockObject) { /* critical section */ }` — locks on ANY specified object for ONLY the critical section. FINER granularity — only the code that accesses shared state is locked. Non-critical code runs without holding the lock. Block is preferred: you control WHICH lock, HOW LONG it's held, and WHAT is protected.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** **Synchronized method** = locking the ENTIRE bank branch (the whole object) every time ONE teller needs to access the vault. Nobody can do ANYTHING — not even use the photocopier — until the vault operation finishes. **Synchronized block** = locking ONLY the vault door (specific lock object) for ONLY the time you're inside the vault. Other tellers can use the photocopier, answer phones, serve customers at other counters — everything outside the vault continues.

**One line to remember:** Synchronized method = locks `this` for entire method (coarse). Synchronized block = locks specific object for specific code (fine). Block preferred — shorter lock time, specific lock, better concurrency.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The account service used `synchronized` methods for both balance updates AND statement generation.** Statement generation took 500ms (reads from DB, formats PDF). Balance updates took 1ms. Because both were `synchronized void`, ANY balance update was blocked while a statement was generating — 500ms delay for a 1ms operation! Fix: separate locks — `balanceLock` for balance operations, `statementLock` for statement generation. Or even better: synchronized block only around `balance.subtract()` (1ms lock hold time instead of 500ms).
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
mvn clean test
# SyncMethodVsBlockTest: 3 tests — all pass!
```
sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1 (Coarse — synchronized method).** Thread-1 calls `debit()` → acquires lock on `this` → sleep(100ms) for validation → subtract balance → release lock. During those 100ms: Thread-2 calls `getBalance()` → BLOCKED waiting for the same `this` lock. Total getBalance wait: ~100ms.

**Step 2 (Fine — synchronized block).** Thread-1 calls `debit()` → sleep(100ms) for validation (NO lock held!) → acquires `balanceLock` → subtract balance (1ms) → release lock. During the 100ms sleep: Thread-2 calls `getBalance()` → acquires `balanceLock` instantly (not held during sleep!) → returns balance. Total getBalance wait: ~0ms.

**Step 3.** 100 threads debit Rs.1000 each from Rs.100,000. With synchronized block: all 100 debits are thread-safe. Final balance: exactly Rs.0.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ SYNCHRONIZED METHOD (coarse) ═══

  debit() { ← LOCK acquired on 'this'
      validateAmount();  ← locked (unnecessary!)
      logTransaction();  ← locked (unnecessary!)
      balance -= amount; ← locked (NEEDED)
      notifyAudit();     ← locked (unnecessary!)
  } ← LOCK released
  Other threads BLOCKED for entire duration (~500ms)!

  ═══ SYNCHRONIZED BLOCK (fine) ═══

  debit() {
      validateAmount();  ← NO lock (runs freely!)
      logTransaction();  ← NO lock (runs freely!)
      synchronized(balanceLock) {
          balance -= amount; ← locked (1ms only!)
      }
      notifyAudit();     ← NO lock (runs freely!)
  }
  Other threads blocked for only 1ms!
```

```
  │    }                                  │

  │    synchronized(balanceLock) {       │ NOT blocked by validate!
  │      return balance                  │
  │    }                                  │

  SOLID: Single Responsibility — lock protects ONLY balance state.
  Pattern: Fine-grained locking — minimize lock hold time.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A synchronized method locks on `this` (or `Class` for static) for the ENTIRE method body — simple but coarse. A synchronized block locks on a specified object for ONLY the critical section — fine-grained, shorter lock hold time, better concurrency. Synchronized block is preferred because: you choose the lock object (dedicated lock instead of `this`), you minimize lock duration (only the critical section, not validation/logging), and different operations can use different locks (balance operations and statement generation don't block each other).

The key metric is LOCK HOLD TIME. Synchronized method: lock held for the entire method including non-critical code (validation, logging, notification). Synchronized block: lock held only for the shared state modification. In banking: account service with 5K operations/sec — synchronized method on debit() holds the lock for 500ms (includes DB query, PDF generation). Synchronized block holds the lock for 1ms (only balance subtraction). The difference: 10 ops/sec (coarse) vs 5,000 ops/sec (fine). Always lock the MINIMUM code for the MINIMUM time.

answers.question: Synchronization — intrinsic monitors (object-level locks) prevent race conditions
answers.shortTitle: Synchronization — intrinsic monitors (object-level locks) prevent race conditions

s1_definition.profdef: Synchronization is Java's mechanism for controlling access to shared resources by multiple threads. Every Java object has an **intrinsic monitor lock** (also called monitor or mutex). When a thread enters a `synchronized` block/method, it ACQUIRES the monitor lock. Other threads trying to acquire the SAME lock are BLOCKED until the first thread releases it (exits the synchronized block). This guarantees **mutual exclusion** (only one thread in the critical section) and **visibility** (changes made by one thread are visible to the next thread that acquires the same lock). Without synchronization: race conditions — two threads read-modify-write the same variable simultaneously, producing corrupt results.
s1_definition.analogy: Every object in Java has an invisible PADLOCK. `synchronized(account)` = grab the padlock. Only ONE person can hold the padlock at a time. Other people trying to grab it WAIT in line (BLOCKED). When you release the padlock (exit synchronized), the next person in line grabs it. This prevents two tellers from simultaneously modifying Rajesh's balance — one waits while the other finishes. Without the padlock: Teller-1 reads balance Rs.100,000, Teller-2 reads Rs.100,000, both debit Rs.50,000, both write Rs.50,000. Expected Rs.0, got Rs.50,000. Rs.50,000 LOST.
s1_definition.oneliner: Every Java object has an intrinsic monitor lock. synchronized = acquire lock → mutual exclusion + visibility. Only ONE thread in critical section at a time. Others BLOCKED until lock released.
s1_definition.raw:

Every Java object has an **intrinsic monitor lock** (also called monitor or mutex). When a thread enters a `synchronized` block/method, it ACQUIRES the monitor lock. Other threads trying to acquire the SAME lock are BLOCKED until the first thread releases it (exits the synchronized block). This guarantees **mutual exclusion** (only one thread in the critical section) and **visibility** (changes made by one thread are visible to the next thread that acquires the same lock). Without synchronization: race conditions — two threads read-modify-write the same variable simultaneously, producing corrupt results.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Every object in Java has an invisible PADLOCK. `synchronized(account)` = grab the padlock. Only ONE person can hold the padlock at a time. Other people trying to grab it WAIT in line (BLOCKED). When you release the padlock (exit synchronized), the next person in line grabs it. This prevents two tellers from simultaneously modifying Rajesh's balance — one waits while the other finishes. Without the padlock: Teller-1 reads balance Rs.100,000, Teller-2 reads Rs.100,000, both debit Rs.50,000, both write Rs.50,000. Expected Rs.0, got Rs.50,000. Rs.50,000 LOST.

**One line to remember:** Every Java object has an intrinsic monitor lock. synchronized = acquire lock → mutual exclusion + visibility. Only ONE thread in critical section at a time. Others BLOCKED until lock released.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's real-time fund transfer service had a race condition.** Two simultaneous transfers from Rajesh's account (Rs.100,000 balance): Transfer-1 debits Rs.60,000, Transfer-2 debits Rs.50,000. Without synchronization: both read balance=100,000, both succeed, balance becomes Rs.50,000 or Rs.40,000 instead of rejecting one transfer (insufficient funds after the first). Fix: `synchronized` on the account object ensures only one transfer executes at a time. Transfer-1 debits → balance=40,000 → Transfer-2 checks → 40,000 < 50,000 → REJECTED. Correct behavior.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Rajesh's account has Rs.100,000. Two transfer threads start simultaneously.

**Step 2.** Thread-1 enters `synchronized void debit(60000)` → acquires monitor lock on the SafeAccount object. Thread-2 tries to enter `synchronized void debit(50000)` → lock held by Thread-1 → Thread-2 state = BLOCKED.

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Java Object Monitor ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │     Java Object (any object)         │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────── │
  │  Object Header:                      │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ Mark Word (64 bits):            │ │
  │  │  - lock state (unlocked/biased/ │ │
  │  │    lightweight/heavyweight)     │ │
  │  │  - owning thread ID            │ │
  │  │  - hash code (when unlocked)   │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ Monitor:                        │ │
  │  │  - owner: Thread (or null)      │ │
  │  │  - entrySet: [BLOCKED threads]  │ │
  │  │  - waitSet: [WAITING threads]   │ │
  │  │  - recursion count: int         │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  synchronized(obj):
  1. Check Mark Word lock state
  2. If unlocked → set owner = currentThread → enter
  3. If owned by currentThread → recursion++ (reentrant!)
  4. If owned by other → thread → entrySet (BLOCKED)
  5. Exit synchronized → owner = null → wake one from entrySet

  Lock escalation:
  No contention → Biased lock (zero overhead)
  Low contention → Lightweight lock (CAS spin)
  High contention → Heavyweight lock (OS mutex, thread parking)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Synchronization prevents race conditions by ensuring mutual exclusion — only one thread can execute a `synchronized` block on the same object at a time. Every Java object has an intrinsic monitor (built into the object header's Mark Word). When a thread enters `synchronized(obj)`, it acquires the monitor lock. Other threads trying to acquire the same lock are BLOCKED until it's released. The monitor also guarantees visibility: changes made inside the synchronized block are visible to the next thread that acquires the same lock (happens-before relationship).

The JVM optimizes monitor locks through lock escalation: biased locking (zero overhead when only one thread ever locks the object), lightweight locking (CAS-based for low contention), and heavyweight locking (OS mutex for high contention). The monitor has two sets: the entry set (BLOCKED threads waiting to acquire) and the wait set (WAITING threads that called wait()). In banking: fund transfer must be synchronized per account — two simultaneous debits on the same account without sync can cause lost updates (balance corruption). With sync: one transfer executes, the other checks the updated balance and may be rejected if insufficient.

answers.question: Designing a thread-safe class — immutable, confinement, delegation, locking strategies
answers.shortTitle: Designing a thread-safe class — immutable, confinement, delegation, locking strategies

s1_definition.profdef: A thread-safe class can be safely used by multiple threads simultaneously without data corruption. Four strategies IN ORDER OF PREFERENCE: (1) **Immutability** — no mutable state at all. If nothing changes, nothing can be corrupted. Best strategy. (String, LocalDate, records with immutable fields). (2) **Confinement** — mutable state is NEVER shared. Each thread has its own copy: stack variables, `ThreadLocal`. No sharing = no race condition. (3) **Delegation** — delegate to existing thread-safe classes: `ConcurrentHashMap`, `AtomicInteger`, `LongAdder`, `BlockingQueue`. Let experts handle synchronization. (4) **Locking** — guard all shared mutable state with a consistent lock: `synchronized(privateFinalLock)`. Last resort — error-prone, reduces concurrency.
s1_definition.analogy: (1) **Immutable** = the bank statement is PRINTED on paper. Nobody can change it. Pass it to 100 people — zero risk. (2) **Confinement** = each teller has their OWN calculator. Nobody shares. No fights over the calculator. (3) **Delegation** = the bank buys a professional SAFE (ConcurrentHashMap) built by experts with built-in security. Don't build your own safe. (4) **Locking** = you build a custom safe with your own padlock. Works, but you might forget to lock it, or hold the key too long. Last resort.
s1_definition.oneliner: Thread safety (best to worst): Immutable (no state to corrupt) → Confinement (no sharing) → Delegation (ConcurrentHashMap/Atomic) → Locking (synchronized). Always prefer the simplest strategy.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Designing a thread-safe class follows four strategies in preference order. First, IMMUTABILITY — if nothing changes, nothing can corrupt. Records with immutable fields (String, BigDecimal, LocalDateTime) are freely shareable with zero synchronization. Second, CONFINEMENT — mutable state that is never shared. Stack-local variables and ThreadLocal give each thread its own copy. Third, DELEGATION — use existing thread-safe classes (ConcurrentHashMap, AtomicInteger, BlockingQueue) instead of writing your own synchronization. Zero `synchronized` in your code — experts handle thread safety. Fourth and last resort, LOCKING — `synchronized(privateFinalLock)` guards shared mutable state. Keep critical sections small, use a private final lock object (never `this`), and document which lock guards which state.

Anti-patterns to avoid: `synchronized(this)` exposes the lock externally (deadlock risk). `synchronized(new Object())` creates a new lock every time (no synchronization!). Leaking mutable internal state via getters (return `List.copyOf()` instead). Publishing `this` during construction (another thread sees a half-built object). In banking: trade confirmation is an immutable record (strategy 1). Date formatting uses ThreadLocal (strategy 2). Trade cache uses ConcurrentHashMap (strategy 3). Balance update uses private final lock (strategy 4 — only for complex multi-field updates).

answers.question: Static synchronized vs instance synchronized — different locks, can run simultaneously
answers.shortTitle: Static synchronized vs instance synchronized — different locks, can run simultaneously

s1_definition.profdef: A `static synchronized` method locks on the **Class object** (`ClassName.class`). An `instance synchronized` method locks on the **instance** (`this`). These are TWO DIFFERENT locks — so they can execute SIMULTANEOUSLY. A thread calling a static synchronized method does NOT block a thread calling an instance synchronized method on the same object, and vice versa. This surprises many developers who assume "synchronized = only one thread in any synchronized method." That's only true for methods using the SAME lock object.
s1_definition.analogy: The bank has TWO padlocks: one on the MAIN VAULT DOOR (Class lock — shared by all branches) and one on RAJESH'S DRAWER (instance lock — specific to Rajesh's account). A teller locking the vault door does NOT prevent another teller from opening Rajesh's drawer — they're different padlocks. Both operations happen simultaneously. Only when two tellers try to lock the SAME padlock does one wait.
s1_definition.oneliner: static synchronized = locks Class object. instance synchronized = locks `this`. DIFFERENT locks → run in PARALLEL. Same lock type → mutual exclusion.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A `static synchronized` method locks on the **Class object** (`ClassName.class`). An `instance synchronized` method locks on the **instance** (`this`). These are TWO DIFFERENT locks — so they can execute SIMULTANEOUSLY. A thread calling a static synchronized method does NOT block a thread calling an instance synchronized method on the same object, and vice versa. This surprises many developers who assume "synchronized = only one thread in any synchronized method." That's only true for methods using the SAME lock object.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The bank has TWO padlocks: one on the MAIN VAULT DOOR (Class lock — shared by all branches) and one on RAJESH'S DRAWER (instance lock — specific to Rajesh's account). A teller locking the vault door does NOT prevent another teller from opening Rajesh's drawer — they're different padlocks. Both operations happen simultaneously. Only when two tellers try to lock the SAME padlock does one wait.

**One line to remember:** static synchronized = locks Class object. instance synchronized = locks `this`. DIFFERENT locks → run in PARALLEL. Same lock type → mutual exclusion.

Fix: use the SAME lock for both: `private static final Object GLOBAL_LOCK = new Object()` — both methods synchronize on GLOBAL_LOCK.

**Step 1.** Thread-1 calls `AccountService.globalAudit()` → acquires lock on `AccountService.class` → holds for 500ms.

**Step 2.** Thread-2 calls `service.debit(1000)` → tries to acquire lock on `this` (the instance) → DIFFERENT lock from Class → acquires immediately → debit executes in <1ms. NOT blocked by the static method!

**Step 3.** Thread-3 calls `service.getBalance()` → tries to acquire lock on `this` → SAME lock as debit() → if debit is running, Thread-3 is BLOCKED.

**Step 4.** Thread-4 calls `priya.debit(2000)` on a DIFFERENT instance → lock on `priya` (different object) → NOT blocked by `rajesh.debit()`. Different instances = different locks = parallel.

```
  ─────────────────────────  ──────────────────────── ─────────── ─────────

  instance sync (obj1)       instance sync (obj1)      YES (same this)    NO!
  instance sync (obj1)       instance sync (obj2)      NO (diff this)     YES!
  static sync (ClassA)       static sync (ClassA)      YES (same Class)   NO!
  static sync (ClassA)       static sync (ClassB)      NO (diff Class)    YES!

  ═══ TWO DIFFERENT LOCKS ═══
```

```
  │    AccountService.class object       │  ← ONE per JVM
  │  Monitor: {                          │
  │    owner: Thread-1 (globalAudit)     │
  │    entrySet: [Thread-3]              │  static sync methods wait here

  │  }                                    │

  Thread-1 holds CLASS lock → does NOT block Thread-2 (holds INSTANCE lock)
  Thread-2 holds INSTANCE lock → does NOT block Thread-1 (holds CLASS lock)

  FIX (if mutual exclusion needed across both):
  private static final Object SHARED_LOCK = new Object();
  static void globalAudit() { synchronized(SHARED_LOCK) { ... } }
  void debit(amt)            { synchronized(SHARED_LOCK) { ... } }
  // Now BOTH methods use the SAME lock → mutual exclusion!
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A static synchronized method locks on the Class object (`ClassName.class`). An instance synchronized method locks on `this` (the specific instance). These are TWO DIFFERENT locks — so a static synchronized method and an instance synchronized method CAN execute simultaneously on the same object. This surprises many developers who expect synchronized to mean "only one thread in any synchronized method." That's only true for methods sharing the SAME lock.

The lock matrix: static sync + static sync (same class) → same Class lock → blocked. Instance sync + instance sync (same object) → same `this` lock → blocked. Instance sync on obj1 + instance sync on obj2 → different `this` → parallel. Static sync + instance sync → different locks (Class vs this) → parallel. In banking: if globalAudit() (static sync) needs to prevent debits (instance sync) during the report, both must use the SAME lock object — not rely on default Class vs instance locks. Fix: `private static final Object SHARED_LOCK` used by both methods.

answers.question: Banking app — synchronized for concurrent account access (method vs block, real scenarios)
answers.shortTitle: Banking app — synchronized for concurrent account access (method vs block, real scenarios)

s1_definition.profdef: In a banking application where multiple users (threads) access the SAME account concurrently, you must synchronize ALL operations that read-and-modify the balance to prevent race conditions. Two approaches: **Synchronized method** — `synchronized void debit()` locks on the Account object for the entire method. Simple but coarse — blocks ALL account operations during ANY operation. **Synchronized block** — `synchronized(account) { balance -= amount; }` locks only the critical section. Better: validation, logging, notification run WITHOUT holding the lock. For real banking: use **per-account locks** (not a global lock) so operations on different accounts run in parallel. For transfers between TWO accounts: acquire locks in CONSISTENT ORDER (by account ID) to prevent deadlock.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh and Priya both try to withdraw from Rajesh's account simultaneously using ATM and mobile. Without synchronization: both read balance Rs.100,000, both withdraw Rs.60,000, both succeed — balance shows Rs.40,000 instead of rejecting one. With synchronization: ATM transaction LOCKS Rajesh's account → checks balance → debits → UNLOCKS. Mobile transaction waits for the lock → checks updated balance → Rs.40,000 < Rs.60,000 → REJECTED. For transfers: lock Rajesh's account FIRST, then Priya's — always in the same order to prevent both sides waiting for each other (deadlock).
s1_definition.oneliner: Per-account lock (not global). Sync block > sync method (shorter lock time). Multi-account transfer: lock in consistent order (by ID) to prevent deadlock.

**Step 1.** 100 threads simultaneously debit Rs.1000 from Rajesh (Rs.100,000). Each thread acquires `rajesh.lock`, checks balance, subtracts, releases lock. Serialized per-account. Final: exactly Rs.0.

**Step 2.** Rajesh and Priya operations in PARALLEL — different lock objects. Thread-1 locks rajesh.lock, Thread-2 locks priya.lock — both execute simultaneously.

**Step 3.** Transfer Rajesh→Priya: consistent lock order → lock CUR3001 (Priya, alphabetically first), then lock SAV2001 (Rajesh). Transfer Priya→Rajesh: SAME order → lock CUR3001 first, then SAV2001. No deadlock — both directions acquire locks in the same order.

```
  └──────────────┘          │  Per-Account Locks:           │
                            │  SAV2001 → lock1              │
                            │  CUR3001 → lock2              │
                            │  FD4001  → lock3              │
                            │  10K accounts = 10K locks     │
                            │  = 10K parallel operations!   │
                            │                               │
                            │  Transfer: lock(min_id) →     │
                            │  lock(max_id) → debit+credit  │
                            │  → consistent order = no DL   │
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Per-Account Lock Design ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
  │         Account                    │
  │  ──────────────────────────────── │
  │  - id: String (final)            │
  │  - lock: Object (private final)  │  ← per-instance lock
  │  - balance: BigDecimal           │  guarded by 'lock'
  │  ──────────────────────────────── │
  │  + debit(amount): void           │  synchronized(lock)
  │  + credit(amount): void          │  synchronized(lock)
  │  + getBalance(): BigDecimal      │  synchronized(lock)
  │  + getLock(): Object             │  for external multi-account sync
  └───────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
  │      TransferService               │
  │  ──────────────────────────────── │
  │  + transfer(from, to, amt): void  │
  │    1. order = sort by account ID  │  ← deadlock prevention!
  │    2. synchronized(first.lock)    │
  │    3.   synchronized(second.lock) │
  │    4.     from.balance -= amt     │
  │    5.     to.balance += amt       │
  └───────────────────────────────────┘

  Pattern: Lock Ordering (prevents deadlock)
  SOLID-S: Account manages its own balance. TransferService manages transfer logic.
  SOLID-D: Transfer depends on Account interface, not implementation.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
In a banking app with concurrent account access, use PER-ACCOUNT locks — each Account has its own `private final Object lock`. Operations on different accounts run in PARALLEL (different locks). Operations on the same account are serialized (same lock). Never use a global lock — it makes ALL account operations sequential regardless of which account they access. Use synchronized BLOCKS, not methods — lock only the balance modification, not validation/logging/notification.

For transfers between two accounts: acquire locks in CONSISTENT ORDER (e.g., alphabetically by account ID) to prevent deadlock. Without ordering: Thread-1 locks Rajesh→waits for Priya, Thread-2 locks Priya→waits for Rajesh → DEADLOCK. With ordering: both threads lock CUR3001(Priya) first, then SAV2001(Rajesh) — one waits, gets it after the other finishes → no deadlock. In production banking: combine in-memory per-account locks with database row-level locks (`SELECT FOR UPDATE`) for distributed consistency across multiple JVM instances.

answers.question: Exception inside synchronized block — lock IS released (JVM emits monitorexit on both paths)
answers.shortTitle: Exception inside synchronized block — lock IS released (JVM emits monitorexit on both paths)

s1_definition.profdef: YES — when an exception is thrown inside a `synchronized` block, the lock IS automatically released. The JVM compiler emits TWO `monitorexit` instructions in the bytecode: one for the normal exit path and one for the exceptional exit path. This is unlike `ReentrantLock` where you MUST manually call `lock.unlock()` in a `finally` block — if you forget, the lock is held forever (deadlock). With `synchronized`, the JVM guarantees lock release regardless of how the block exits — normal return, exception, or even Error. This is a major advantage of `synchronized` over manual Lock.
s1_definition.analogy: When a bank teller is inside the vault (synchronized block) and suddenly faints (exception), the vault door AUTOMATICALLY unlocks. The vault has an emergency mechanism (monitorexit on exceptional path) that opens the door regardless of what happens inside. With a manual padlock (ReentrantLock), if the teller faints while holding the key, nobody else can enter — unless someone explicitly takes the key from the teller's hand (finally { lock.unlock() }).
s1_definition.oneliner: synchronized: JVM auto-releases lock on exception (two monitorexit in bytecode — normal + exceptional). ReentrantLock: YOU must release in finally. Forget = permanent deadlock.
s1_definition.raw:

The JVM compiler emits TWO `monitorexit` instructions in the bytecode: one for the normal exit path and one for the exceptional exit path. This is unlike `ReentrantLock` where you MUST manually call `lock.unlock()` in a `finally` block — if you forget, the lock is held forever (deadlock). With `synchronized`, the JVM guarantees lock release regardless of how the block exits — normal return, exception, or even Error. This is a major advantage of `synchronized` over manual Lock.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When a bank teller is inside the vault (synchronized block) and suddenly faints (exception), the vault door AUTOMATICALLY unlocks. The vault has an emergency mechanism (monitorexit on exceptional path) that opens the door regardless of what happens inside. With a manual padlock (ReentrantLock), if the teller faints while holding the key, nobody else can enter — unless someone explicitly takes the key from the teller's hand (finally { lock.unlock() }).

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The settlement service used ReentrantLock without a finally block.** When a `SettlementException` was thrown during processing, `lock.unlock()` was never called. The lock was held permanently. All subsequent settlement threads were BLOCKED forever — 500 pending trades stuck. The on-call engineer had to restart the service at 2 AM. Fix option 1: add `finally { lock.unlock() }`. Fix option 2 (simpler): switch to `synchronized` — JVM handles lock release automatically, no risk of forgetting.

```bash
mvn clean test
# ExceptionInSyncTest: 4 tests — all pass!
```
sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Thread-1 enters `synchronized(lock)` → JVM executes `monitorenter` → lock acquired.

**Step 2.** Inside the block, `debit()` throws RuntimeException. Method exits abnormally.

**Step 3.** JVM hits the exceptional exit path → executes `monitorexit` (auto-generated by compiler) → lock RELEASED. Exception propagates up the call stack.

**Step 4.** Thread-2 tries `synchronized(lock)` → lock is free (Thread-1 released it) → acquires lock → enters block successfully.

**Step 5.** With ReentrantLock WITHOUT finally: Thread-1 calls `lock.lock()`, exception thrown, `lock.unlock()` never reached → lock permanently held → Thread-2 waits FOREVER → DEADLOCK.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ SYNCHRONIZED: auto-release on exception ═══

  Thread-1:
    monitorenter(lock) ✅
    → debit() → THROWS RuntimeException!
    monitorexit(lock) ✅ ← JVM auto-releases! (exceptional path)
    → exception propagates

  Thread-2:
    monitorenter(lock) ✅ ← lock is free! Acquired!

  ═══ ReentrantLock WITHOUT finally: lock STUCK ═══

  Thread-1:
    lock.lock() ✅
    → debit() → THROWS RuntimeException!
    lock.unlock() ← NEVER REACHED!
    → lock HELD FOREVER!

  Thread-2:
    lock.lock() → BLOCKED FOREVER! DEADLOCK!

  ═══ FIX: always use finally ═══
  lock.lock();
  try { debit(); } finally { lock.unlock(); }  ← ALWAYS runs!
```

```
  ═══ HLD — Lock Release Guarantee in Settlement Service ═══

  ┌──────────┐  Kafka   ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Trade    │─────────→│  Settlement Service (50 threads)   │
  │ Events   │          │                                     │
  └──────────┘          │  synchronized(account) {            │
                        │    settle(trade);  // might throw!  │
                        │  }                                   │
                        │  ← JVM: monitorexit on BOTH paths   │
                        │  Exception? Lock still released! ✅  │
                        │  Next thread processes next trade.   │
                        │                                     │
                        │  vs ReentrantLock without finally:   │
                        │  Exception → lock.unlock() skipped  │
                        │  → lock held FOREVER → ALL threads   │
                        │  BLOCKED → service DEAD! ❌          │
                        └─────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Bytecode: monitorenter / monitorexit ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Bytecode for synchronized block:        │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  0: aload_1          (load lock object)  │
  │  1: monitorenter     (acquire lock)      │
  │  2: ... body code ...                    │
  │  8: monitorexit      (normal exit) ───→ return │
  │  9: goto end                             │
  │ 12: astore_2         (exception handler) │
  │ 13: aload_1                              │
  │ 14: monitorexit      (exceptional exit)  │ ← AUTO-GENERATED!
  │ 15: aload_2                              │
  │ 16: athrow           (rethrow exception) │
  │ 17: return                               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  TWO monitorexit instructions:
  Line 8:  normal exit path → lock released
  Line 14: exceptional exit path → lock released
  → Lock ALWAYS released regardless of how block exits!

  ┌────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ReentrantLock (manual)        │
  │  ───────────────────────────── │
  │  + lock(): void                │  NO auto-release!
  │  + unlock(): void              │  MUST call in finally!
  │  + tryLock(): boolean          │  advantage over synchronized
  │  + lockInterruptibly(): void   │  advantage over synchronized
  └────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When an exception is thrown inside a synchronized block, the lock IS automatically released. The JVM compiler generates TWO `monitorexit` instructions in the bytecode — one for the normal exit and one for the exceptional exit. This is a significant advantage of `synchronized` over `ReentrantLock`: you cannot forget to release the lock. With ReentrantLock, `lock.unlock()` must be in a `finally` block — if you forget and an exception is thrown, the lock is held permanently, causing deadlock for all threads waiting on it.

In production: a settlement service using ReentrantLock without `finally { lock.unlock() }` experienced a permanent lock hold when a SettlementException was thrown. All 50 settlement threads were blocked forever. The service had to be restarted. With `synchronized`: the same exception would have auto-released the lock, and the next thread would have picked up the next trade immediately. Rule: prefer `synchronized` for simplicity and safety. Use ReentrantLock only when you need its extra features (tryLock, lockInterruptibly, fairness) — and ALWAYS wrap in try-finally.

answers.question: Why synchronizing on String literal / interned object is a bug — use private final Object lock
answers.shortTitle: Why synchronizing on String literal / interned object is a bug — use private final Object lock

s1_definition.profdef: Synchronizing on a String literal (`synchronized("LOCK")`) is a bug because String literals are **interned** — the JVM maintains a single instance per unique literal in the String pool. If TWO completely unrelated classes both synchronize on `"LOCK"`, they lock on the SAME object — causing unexpected blocking and potential deadlock between code that has nothing to do with each other. Same problem with `Boolean.TRUE`, `Integer.valueOf(1)` (cached -128 to 127), or any shared/interned object. Fix: ALWAYS use `private final Object lock = new Object()` — a dedicated lock object that ONLY your class knows about. Private: no external code can lock on it. Final: can't be reassigned to a different object. New Object: unique to your class.
s1_definition.analogy: Synchronizing on a String literal is like using the FRONT DOOR KEY of the building as your vault key. Every shop in the building has the same front door key. When you lock "your vault" with this key, you're actually locking the ENTIRE BUILDING — other shops can't enter. Two shops trying to lock at the same time → deadlock. Fix: each shop gets its OWN unique key (private final Object) that nobody else has.
s1_definition.oneliner: String literals are interned → SHARED across entire JVM. synchronized("LOCK") = global lock affecting ALL code using "LOCK". Fix: private final Object lock = new Object() — unique, private, not shared.
s1_definition.raw:

Fix: ALWAYS use `private final Object lock = new Object()` — a dedicated lock object that ONLY your class knows about. Private: no external code can lock on it. Final: can't be reassigned to a different object. New Object: unique to your class.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Synchronizing on a String literal is like using the FRONT DOOR KEY of the building as your vault key. Every shop in the building has the same front door key. When you lock "your vault" with this key, you're actually locking the ENTIRE BUILDING — other shops can't enter. Two shops trying to lock at the same time → deadlock. **One line to remember:** String literals are interned → SHARED across entire JVM. synchronized("LOCK") = global lock affecting ALL code using "LOCK". Fix: private final Object lock = new Object() — unique, private, not shared.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — Two unrelated microservices (AccountService and AuditService) in the same JVM both used `synchronized("GLOBAL")`.** The AuditService held the lock for 10 seconds during report generation. During those 10 seconds, AccountService debits were BLOCKED — customers couldn't withdraw money. The services had no intentional relationship — the shared String literal was a coincidence. Fix: each service gets its own `private final Object lock = new Object()`. No accidental sharing.

**Step 3.** Service-A finishes after 500ms → releases lock → Service-B unblocked → enters. Total delay: 500ms for completely unrelated code!

**Step 4.** Fix: each service uses `private final Object lock = new Object()`. Service-A's lock and Service-B's lock are different objects → never block each other → parallel.

```
  Rules: PRIVATE (no external access) + FINAL (no reassign) + new Object (unique)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Synchronizing on a String literal is a bug because String literals are interned — the JVM stores one instance per unique literal in the String pool. If two completely unrelated classes synchronize on `"LOCK"`, they lock on the SAME object, causing unexpected blocking and potential deadlock. The same applies to `Boolean.TRUE`, `Integer.valueOf()` in the cached range (-128 to 127), and any other shared/pooled object.

The fix is `private final Object lock = new Object()`. PRIVATE: no external code can access your lock → no accidental contention from other classes. FINAL: the lock reference can't be reassigned → you always synchronize on the same object (reassigning would silently break synchronization). new Object(): creates a unique instance → not shared with anyone. Also avoid `synchronized(this)` — external code holding a reference to your object can lock on it, causing unexpected blocking. In banking: AccountService and AuditService both used `synchronized("GLOBAL")` → audit report generation blocked all account operations for 10 seconds. Fix: separate private locks.

answers.question: Deadlock — what it is, code example, detection, and prevention strategies
answers.shortTitle: Deadlock — what it is, code example, detection, and prevention strategies

s1_definition.profdef: A **deadlock** occurs when TWO or MORE threads are PERMANENTLY blocked, each waiting for a lock held by the other. Thread-1 holds Lock-A and waits for Lock-B. Thread-2 holds Lock-B and waits for Lock-A. Neither can proceed — the system is FROZEN forever. Four conditions (ALL must be true for deadlock): (1) **Mutual exclusion** — locks are exclusive. (2) **Hold and wait** — thread holds one lock while waiting for another. (3) **No preemption** — locks can't be forcibly taken. (4) **Circular wait** — thread-1 waits for thread-2, thread-2 waits for thread-1. Prevention: break ANY ONE condition — typically break circular wait by always acquiring locks in a CONSISTENT ORDER.
s1_definition.analogy: Teller-1 is inside Rajesh's vault and needs to enter Priya's vault to complete a transfer. Teller-2 is inside Priya's vault and needs to enter Rajesh's vault. Both are waiting for the other to leave. Neither will leave because they need the other vault first. Both stand FROZEN forever. The bank halts. Fix: bank rule — "ALWAYS enter the vault with the lower account number FIRST." Both tellers would enter CUR3001 (Priya) first → no circular wait → no deadlock.
s1_definition.oneliner: Deadlock = two threads, each holding a lock the other needs. Both wait forever. Fix: always acquire locks in CONSISTENT ORDER (by account ID, by object hashCode). Break circular wait.

(4) **Circular wait** — thread-1 waits for thread-2, thread-2 waits for thread-1. Prevention: break ANY ONE condition — typically break circular wait by always acquiring locks in a CONSISTENT ORDER.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Teller-1 is inside Rajesh's vault and needs to enter Priya's vault to complete a transfer. Teller-2 is inside Priya's vault and needs to enter Rajesh's vault. sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The fund transfer service locked accounts in the order received.** Transfer Rajesh→Priya: lock(Rajesh), lock(Priya). Simultaneously, transfer Priya→Rajesh: lock(Priya), lock(Rajesh). DEADLOCK. Both transfers frozen. Customer complaint: "My transfer has been processing for 2 hours." Fix: always lock by account ID order — `CUR3001` before `SAV2001` (alphabetical). Both transfers: lock(CUR3001/Priya) first, then lock(SAV2001/Rajesh). No circular wait. No deadlock.

**Step 2.** Thread-1: lock(Priya) → BLOCKED (held by Thread-2). Thread-2: lock(Rajesh) → BLOCKED (held by Thread-1). DEADLOCK! Both wait FOREVER.

**Step 3 (Fix).** Both threads: lock(CUR3001/Priya) first, then lock(SAV2001/Rajesh). Thread-1: lock(Priya) ✅ → lock(Rajesh) ✅ → transfer → unlock both. Thread-2: lock(Priya) → WAITS → Thread-1 finishes → Thread-2 gets Priya → gets Rajesh → transfer → done. Sequential but CORRECT. No deadlock.

```
  ═══ DEADLOCK ═══

  Thread-1: lock(Rajesh) ✅ ──→ lock(Priya) BLOCKED! ←─── held by Thread-2
  Thread-2: lock(Priya) ✅ ──→ lock(Rajesh) BLOCKED! ←─── held by Thread-1
  CIRCULAR WAIT → DEADLOCK! Both frozen forever!

  ═══ FIX: CONSISTENT ORDERING ═══

  Thread-1: lock(CUR3001) ✅ → lock(SAV2001) ✅ → transfer → unlock both
  Thread-2: lock(CUR3001) WAITS ──→ gets it → lock(SAV2001) ✅ → transfer
  NO circular wait → NO deadlock!

  ═══ FOUR CONDITIONS (ALL must be true) ═══
  1. Mutual exclusion    → locks are exclusive
  2. Hold and wait       → hold one, wait for another
  3. No preemption       → can't force-take locks
  4. Circular wait       → A waits B, B waits A
  Break ANY ONE → no deadlock. Easiest: break #4 with consistent ordering.
```

```
  │  holds: A    │──waits→│  holds: B    │
  │  wants: B    │←waits──│  wants: A    │
  └──────────────┘        └──────────────┘

  │      }                                │
  │    }                                  │

  2. tryLock(timeout): back off if can't acquire → break hold-and-wait
  3. Single lock: one lock for all → break hold-and-wait (but kills concurrency)
  4. Lock-free: AtomicInteger, ConcurrentHashMap → break mutual exclusion
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A deadlock occurs when two or more threads permanently block each other — each holds a lock the other needs. Four conditions must ALL be true: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Prevention: break any one condition. The most practical strategy is breaking circular wait through consistent lock ordering — always acquire locks in the same order (by account ID, object hash, or any deterministic ordering).

Detection: `jstack <PID>` prints "Found one Java-level deadlock" with the exact threads and locks involved. Programmatically: `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` returns involved thread IDs.
